"I tell you, he went in there," Willa insisted, pointing a dramatic finger at the old clock tower. "With that little black case and everything!"

"He probably just went to check the time," Leo replied, leaning back against the park bench. "Mr. Gable is the town jeweler, Willa. Clocks are his business."

"At nine o'clock at night? And did you see how he looked around first? Like he was afraid of being followed!"

"You're being dramatic. It's a clear night. Maybe he just wanted to look at the stars from the top."

"Then why did the light in the belfry just go on, and then off again, three times?" Willa shot back, her eyes gleaming with excitement. "It was a signal, Leo! I'll bet my entire allowance on it."

"A signal for what? For the other jewelers to start their secret meeting?" Leo chuckled. "You've been reading too many of those detective novels again."

"Laugh if you want to," Willa said, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "But my father says that Mr. Gable has been acting strangely ever since that new fellow, Mr. Corbin, came to town. He's barely been in his own shop."

"Maybe he's sick."

"Or maybe he's involved in something!" Willa declared. "Something that requires secret meetings in a clock tower!"

"Quiet!" Leo warned, grabbing her arm. "Look!"

The small door at the base of the tower creaked open. Mr. Corbin, the newcomer with the slick black hair and expensive suit, stepped out into the shadows. He glanced around quickly before melting into the darkness of Elm Street. A minute later, Mr. Gable himself emerged, looking pale and flustered. He scurried in the opposite direction, his head down.

"You see!" Willa whispered triumphantly. "Now do you believe me?"

"I admit it's odd," Leo conceded. "But what could they possibly be doing?"

"That's what we are going to find out," Willa said, her mind already racing. "Tomorrow, we're going to pay a visit to that clock tower."

The next afternoon, the children found the clock tower door unlocked. An ancient, musty smell of dust and oil met them as they stepped inside. A narrow, winding staircase spiraled up into the darkness above.

"I don't like this, Willa," Leo said, peering nervously into the gloom. "It feels spooky."

"Nonsense, it's an adventure!" she replied, already starting up the steps. "Come on!"

They climbed in silence, their footsteps echoing on the old wood. When they reached the belfry, they found a dusty room filled with enormous gears and wheels. Sunlight streamed through the four large clock faces, illuminating dust motes dancing in the air. In the center of the room, on a small crate, sat a half-eaten sandwich and a folded newspaper.

"See? Nothing," Leo said, relieved. "Someone just had their lunch up here."

"Wait a minute," Willa said, picking up the newspaper. It was folded to a page filled with classified advertisements. Several of them had been circled in red ink.

"What is it?" Leo asked, leaning over her shoulder.

The circled ads were strange. "Bluebird seeks a new cage. Ready to fly at noon." Another read, "Lost canary. Sings a lovely tune. Reward offered."

"It's a code!" Willa breathed. "Mr. Gable isn't a spy. He's helping someone escape!"

"Escape from what?"

"I don't know yet. But these messages are how they communicate!"

"Good afternoon, children."

The voice made them both jump. A police officer stood in the entryway to the belfry, his arms crossed. It was Officer Miller.

"I thought I might find someone up here," he said, his expression unreadable. "This tower is supposed to be locked."

"We, uh, we were just exploring," Leo stammered.

Officer Miller's eyes fell on the newspaper in Willa's hand. "Finding anything interesting?"

"Just an old paper," Willa said quickly, trying to hide it behind her back.

"I see," the officer said slowly. "You know, we've been getting reports about strange lights up here at night. And Mr. Gable has been a person of interest for some time." He took a step closer. "He's not a bad man, you understand. Just a little too trusting. Some people take advantage of that."

"Like Mr. Corbin?" Willa blurted out.

Officer Miller's eyebrows shot up. "What do you know about Mr. Corbin?"

"We saw him here last night! With Mr. Gable!" Willa explained. "We think they're using coded messages in the newspaper to help someone!"

The officer looked from Willa's earnest face to Leo's worried one. A slow smile spread across his face. "You two have certainly been busy. As it happens, you're not entirely wrong. But this isn't a job for amateurs." He gently took the newspaper from Willa's hand. "Why don't you let me take it from here? And you two can go get some ice cream. My treat."

Yes, some of them are. They slip over the border and make their way to coastal areas just like this one." Jerry's expression was grim. "We believe B4 is the key figure in a very organized escape route."

"And you think his station is located right here, near Sunset Beach?" Penny pressed, her eyes wide with excitement.

"The triangulation from our last intercepts points to this general vicinity," Jerry confirmed. "That's why we're here. We wait for him to transmit, and then we pounce. But he's clever. He only broadcasts for a minute or two at a time, and never from the same place twice."

"A mobile station!" Penny exclaimed.

"Exactly. That's why Mr. Voice from the Cave is so hard to pin down." Jerry glanced at his watch. "Well, girls, I'm afraid the tour is over. I need to get back to the Inn, and you two should probably get out of those damp clothes."

He led them back through the hedge to the waiting taxi. The ride back to the Crystal Inn was mostly silent, but Penny's mind was racing faster than the car's engine. Spies, escaped prisoners, a secret radio station! It was all happening right under their noses. And somehow, she felt certain that the cold, mysterious Mrs. Deline was tangled up in the whole affair.

"I don't care what she said," Penny declared as soon as they were safely back in their hotel room. "I simply don't believe that story about the fish bones!"

"But Penny, she saw us digging," Louise reasoned, toweling her damp hair. "She had to say something. It was the perfect way to make us look silly and stop us from searching."

"That's just it!" Penny whirled around, her face alight with a new theory. "It was too perfect! She wanted us to stop digging because the package isn't garbage! It's something important, I know it is!"

"Then why tell us what she buried? Why not just let us get tired and give up?"

"Because she's playing a deeper game, Lou! And what about the writing on her skirt? We both saw her!"

"We thought we saw her," Louise corrected gently. "There wasn't a mark on it."

"Invisible ink!" Penny insisted, snapping her fingers. "I said it before and I'm more certain than ever now. She wrote something on that skirt, and it was a message!"

"Oh, Penny, you and your imagination," Louise sighed, but a flicker of interest showed in her eyes. "Even if you were right, how would we ever prove it? We can't very well ask to borrow her suit."

An idea, bold and outrageous, began to form in Penny's mind. "Maybe we don't have to ask," she said slowly, a mischievous glint in her eye. "The suit was white flannel, and it got damp in the rain. What does a person do with a damp, sandy flannel suit?"

"They'd have it cleaned," Louise answered, her own eyes beginning to widen as she followed Penny's train of thought. "The hotel laundry service!"

"Precisely! All we have to do is watch for the laundry pickup from her room. If we can intercept that skirt, even for just a few minutes, we might be able to solve this whole mystery."

"Intercept it? Penny, that's stealing!" Louise gasped, aghast.

"It's not stealing if we give it right back," Penny argued logically. "It's just borrowing for a good cause. Think of it, Lou! We could be helping Jerry and the Army!"

Louise looked doubtful, but Penny's enthusiasm was, as always, contagious. The plan was risky, but the thought of uncovering a real spy message was too thrilling to resist.

They spent the next hour planning. Their strategy centered on the service corridor where the hotel staff collected laundry bags left outside the guests' doors each morning. Louise, who was less likely to arouse suspicion, would post herself near the corridor with a book, pretending to read. Penny would wait in their room, armed with a small travel iron they had packed.

The next morning, their nerves were on edge. Louise took up her post by a potted fern that offered a good view of the hallway. Penny paced their room, checking the iron's plug for the tenth time. It seemed like an eternity before a maid appeared at the far end of the hall, pushing a large canvas cart. As she approached Mrs. Deline's room, number 214, she paused. The door opened a crack, and a white flannel skirt was placed neatly atop a laundry bag just outside the door.

This was the signal. Louise, her heart pounding, waited until the maid had moved on to the next room. Then she sprang into action. With a casual air she hoped was convincing, she walked toward room 214. Just as she reached it, she feigned a clumsy stumble, sending her book skittering across the floor.

"Oh, bother!" she cried, bending down. As she gathered the pages of her book, she deftly snatched the white skirt from the laundry bag, bundling it under her arm. In a flash, she was back on her feet and hurrying toward her own room, her face flushed with the success of her daring maneuver.

"I've got it!" she whispered, bursting through the door and tossing the skirt to Penny. "But we have to be quick! The maid will be back this way soon!"

Penny spread the garment out on the desk, her hands trembling slightly. "Now for the moment of truth," she breathed. She plugged in the iron and waited for it to heat up. According to the mystery novels she had read, heat was the simplest way to reveal messages written in lemon juice, the most common form of invisible ink.

"Be careful not to burn it," Louise warned, peering anxiously over her shoulder.

Gently, Penny pressed the hot iron against the fabric of the skirt, near the hem where they had seen Mrs. Deline writing. For a second, nothing happened. Penny's heart sank. Had she been wrong all along?

Then, as if by magic, faint brownish lines began to appear on the white flannel.

"It's working!" Louise shrieked in a hushed whisper. "You were right, Penny! You were right!"

Penny moved the iron carefully over the area. More letters and numbers materialized from the heat. It was not a map, but a short, cryptic sequence: D-F-7-N-E-S-W.

"D-F-7-N-E-S-W," Penny read aloud, her brow furrowed in concentration. "What on earth could that mean?"

"Drift Fence Seven?" Louise suggested. "We saw numbered posts on that long fence by the dunes."

"Of course! The drift fence!" Penny's face lit up. "And N-E-S-W must be directions. North, East, South, West. It's a set of instructions for digging!"

"We have to put the skirt back!" Louise urged, glancing nervously at the door.

Penny quickly took a photograph of the markings with her small camera, a precaution she had insisted upon. Then, folding the skirt just as it had been, Louise crept back into the hallway. The coast was clear. In a moment, she had replaced the skirt on the laundry bag outside room 214, her mission accomplished without anyone being the wiser.

"Now what?" she asked, returning to the room, still breathless from the excitement.

"Now," Penny declared, grabbing her jacket, "we go back to the beach. This time, we know exactly where to dig."

The sky was still overcast from the previous day's storm, and a cool wind blew in off the grey sea as the girls made their way back to the dunes. They found the long drift fence easily enough and began walking along it, counting the posts.

"One, two, three..." Penny counted. "Here it is! Post number seven!"

They stood before the marker, looking at the chaotic jumble of sand dunes that stretched before them. "Now for the directions," Penny said, consulting her memory of the code. "N-E-S-W. It doesn't make any sense as a direction. North-East-South-West?"

"Maybe it's not a path to follow, but the number of steps to take," Louise mused. "Like, nine steps north, then east, then south, then west?"

"Nine? Where did you get nine?"

"I don't know, it just sounded right!"

Penny shook her head. "No, it must be simpler. N-E-S-W. Maybe it's a pattern. Let's start from the post. North... that's toward the hotel. Let's take ten paces." She paced it off. "Now East... toward the water." She took ten more paces. "Now South... back toward the fence." Ten more. "And West... back toward the post." She completed the square. "We're right back where we started from!"

"This is impossible," Louise sighed in frustration. "Maybe it's not directions at all."

Penny stood in the center of the square she had paced, tapping her foot in the sand. Her eyes scanned the dunes, the fence, the post. "Wait a minute, Lou. Look at the post."

Louise looked. It was a simple wooden post with a faded number 7 painted on it. "I don't see anything."

"Not on the post. At the base of it! Look how the sand is disturbed. But not by digging. It looks like something was used to draw in the sand, and then it was brushed over." Penny dropped to her knees. Using her hands, she carefully swept away the top layer of sand around the post. Underneath, four faint letters had been traced and then partially obscured. N. E. S. W. And beside each letter was an arrow. The arrow by N pointed not north, but directly at a specific, cone-shaped dune. The other letters seemed to be decoys.

"This is it!" Penny cried triumphantly. "The message on the skirt wasn't the map itself! It was the key to finding the map! Mrs. Deline drew this, and the code was just to tell the other person which post to look at!"

With renewed energy, the girls scrambled over to the indicated dune. It looked no different from any of the others, but now they were certain. They began to dig, scooping away the damp, heavy sand with their bare hands. For several minutes they worked in a determined silence, broken only by the cry of gulls and the sighing of the wind.

"I think I felt something!" Louise suddenly exclaimed. Her fingers had brushed against something hard and smooth.

Together they cleared away the remaining sand. There, nestled in a hollow, was not a package of fish bones, but a small, watertight metal box. It was heavy for its size and locked with a simple clasp.

Penny's fingers fumbled with the cold metal. With a click, the clasp sprang open. She lifted the lid, her heart thudding against her ribs.

Inside, resting on a bed of dark velvet, was not a codebook or a secret message. It was a strange and intricate piece of machinery, a series of glass tubes and fine copper wires mounted on a small black base.

"What is it?" Louise whispered, staring at the object.

"I'm not sure," Penny answered slowly. "But it looks like a part from some kind of radio. A vacuum tube, maybe? A very specialized one." She remembered Jerry's words about the mobile transmitting station. This had to be a vital component for it.

"We have to take this to Jerry right away!" Louise said urgently, looking around the deserted beach as if spies might suddenly pop up from behind every dune.

"You're right." Penny carefully closed the box. "Let's go."

They had just started to rise to their feet when a shadow fell over them. A cold voice spoke from behind.

"I believe you have something that belongs to me."

The girls froze, then slowly turned. It was Mrs. Deline. She stood a few feet away, her arms crossed, her face a mask of cold fury. She was not alone. Beside her stood a tall, grim-faced man in a dark raincoat, though it was not raining. His eyes, small and hard as pebbles, were fixed on the metal box in Penny's hand.

"We, uh, we were just..." Penny stammered, clutching the box tightly.

"You were just interfering in matters that do not concern you," Mrs. Deline finished, her voice like ice. "Give me the box, child."

"No!" Penny said, taking a step back. "This is evidence! It's for the Army!"

The man in the raincoat took a menacing step forward. "Do not make this difficult," he said in a low voice with a faint, unplaceable accent.

Suddenly, another voice cut through the tense air. "That's far enough!"

Jerry Livingston came striding over the nearest dune, and behind him were two uniformed Coast Guardsmen. Jerry held a small pistol pointed steadily at the man in the raincoat.

"It seems the party is over, B4," Jerry said calmly.

The man's face paled. He looked from Jerry to Mrs. Deline, his expression a mixture of shock and betrayal. "You!" he snarled at her. "You led them here!"

Mrs. Deline did not flinch. "It was my duty," she replied coolly.

The man, B4, made a sudden move, but the two Coast Guardsmen were on him in an instant, pinning his arms behind his back.

Penny and Louise stood by, stunned into silence by the swift turn of events. Jerry walked over to them, a look of relief on his face. "Are you girls alright?"

"Yes, but... Mrs. Deline?" Penny asked in complete bewilderment. "I don't understand. I thought she was a spy!"

A rare smile touched Mrs. Deline's lips. She walked over to Penny. "I apologize for my behavior, Penny," she said, her voice surprisingly warm. "My name is not Deline. I am an agent with Federal intelligence. I was assigned to watch this man, who we knew only as B4. We suspected he was coordinating prisoner escapes, but we needed to catch him receiving a shipment. That shipment was the radio tube you found."

"The fish bones..." Louise murmured.

"A story to put you off the scent," Mrs. Deline confirmed. "You girls were so persistent, I was afraid you would ruin the entire operation. My pretending to write on my skirt was a signal for B4, who was watching from the lighthouse with a spyglass. It told him the drop was made and where to find the key, at post seven. He was meant to pick it up tonight. We were waiting for him."

"So you were on our side all along!" Penny exclaimed, a blush creeping up her cheeks. "And we thought... we stole your skirt!"

Mrs. Deline actually chuckled. "Yes, I know. I saw you, Louise. It was a very clumsy, but effective maneuver. When the skirt was returned with the faint scorch marks on it, I knew you had discovered the invisible ink. I realized you wouldn't give up, so I contacted Jerry. We decided to let you lead us to the box, and we would follow to ensure your safety."

"The package contained a homing device," Jerry added, taking the metal box from Penny. "Once you opened it, it sent a silent signal to a receiver I'm carrying. That's how we knew you'd found it and that B4 had arrived."

"Gosh," Penny said, completely deflated and thrilled at the same time. "So we helped, but only by accident."

"You did more than that," Mrs. Deline said kindly. "Your ingenuity forced our hand, but it also flushed B4 out into the open. You are a remarkable young woman, Penny Parker. Reckless and far too imaginative, but remarkable nonetheless."

Louise beamed at her friend. "She's certainly that," she agreed.

As the Coast Guardsmen led the sullen B4 away, Jerry turned to the girls. "Well, thanks to you two, Mr. Voice from the Cave has been silenced for good. But I think you've had enough excitement for one day. Let's get you back to the hotel. I think you've earned it."

Walking back across the sand, with Jerry and the surprisingly friendly Mrs. Deline, Penny felt a familiar surge of satisfaction. The mystery was solved, the spy was caught, and Sunset Beach was safe once more. And even though she had been wrong about almost everything, in the end, she had been right about the one thing that mattered most. There was a secret to be found in the dunes, and she had been the one to find it.

"The fish bones..." Louise murmured.

He was meant to pick it up tonight. We were waiting for him."

"So you were on our side all along!" Penny exclaimed, a blush creeping up her cheeks. "And we thought... we stole your skirt!"

"Gosh," Penny said, completely deflated and thrilled at the same time. "So we helped, but only by accident."

"You did more than that," Mrs. Deline said kindly. "Your ingenuity forced our hand, but it also flushed B4 out into the open. You are a remarkable young woman, Penny Parker. Reckless and far too imaginative, but remarkable nonetheless."

Louise beamed at her friend. "She's certainly that," she agreed.

Walking back across the sand, with Jerry and the surprisingly friendly Mrs. Deline, Penny felt a familiar surge of satisfaction. The mystery was solved, the spy was caught, and Sunset Beach was safe once more. And even though she had been wrong about almost everything, in the end, she had been right about the one thing that mattered most. There was a secret to be found in the dunes, and she had been the one to find it.

"The Dragon's Tooth is that big shard of rock north of the point. And the Whispering Widow is a sea cave that makes a moanin' sound when the tide comes in. Dangerous places. Full of currents."

"A treasure map," Jerry said, a hint of scorn in his voice. "So the old keeper was a fortune seeker. He probably went out looking for it and got himself into trouble with the tide. That explains his disappearance." He turned to one of his men. "Get the Coast Guard to do a search around those coordinates. But our priority is still Richter and Deline."

"But it might not be about treasure!" Penny protested. "That verse sounds like a warning! And it's all connected to Mrs. Deline, I know it is!"

"Penny, you've done good work," Jerry said, patting her on the shoulder. "But you can't connect everything to your spy theory. Sometimes a missing person is just a missing person. Let the professionals handle it from here."

Penny watched him walk away, feeling a familiar surge of frustration. He wasn't listening! He saw a silly treasure map, but she saw a clue. A clue that McCoy had left behind because he had stumbled onto something far more dangerous than any sunken chest.

"He's wrong, Lou," Penny said fiercely once they were alone. "I know he is."

"But what can we do?" Louise asked. "Jerry won't listen, and Dad will never let us go exploring those dangerous places by ourselves."

"We don't have to explore them," Penny said, a new idea taking shape. "We just have to understand the map better than Jerry does. And I know just who to ask."

Her eyes fell on Jake Skagway, who was still lingering by the door, looking out to sea.

They found him on the pier, mending a net with gnarled, practiced fingers. He looked up as they approached.

"That city fella ain't gonna find Jim," he stated flatly. "Not by lookin' for treasure."

"You don't think it's a treasure map either?" Penny asked eagerly.

Jake snorted. "Jim McCoy weren't interested in gold. He was interested in one thing: that light. And the sea. He knew every rock and current in these waters. That ain't a map for findin' somethin'. It's a map for avoidin' somethin'. Or for trackin' it."

He pointed a finger at the verse which Penny had copied into her notebook. "Whispering Widow's near. That cave ain't just one cave. It's a whole network. Goes deep into the cliffs. Locals stay clear. They call it the 'back door' to the beach, 'cause you can get from the water to the woods inland without bein' seen, if you know the way."

A back door. The words electrified Penny's thoughts. A secret route from the sea to the land. A way to get past the Coast Guard patrols her father had mentioned.

"Mrs. Deline's accomplice!" Penny gasped. "Karl Richter! He's still out there! The big escape from the main cave was a diversion, but what if he was the only one who didn't get caught? What if he's hiding in those caves, waiting for a chance to escape by sea?"

"And Mr. McCoy found out," Louise added, catching on. "He saw something, maybe a boat, or lights. So he made this chart for himself, to mark the spy's hiding place!"

"And Richter caught him," Penny finished grimly. "The 'treasure' in the verse wasn't gold. It was a person! A spy! That's what's 'more than silver, more than gold' to the enemy!"

"Now you're thinkin'," Jake grunted, giving a firm tug on his net. "That's why Jim's gone. He got too close to the real treasure."

A cold dread washed over Penny. If their theory was correct, Jim McCoy was a prisoner, and his time was running out.

"We have to tell Jerry!" Louise exclaimed.

"He won't believe us," Penny said, shaking her head. "He thinks it's a treasure hunt gone wrong. He'll waste hours searching the open water. By the time he realizes the truth, Richter and his prisoner could be gone."

"So what do we do?" Louise asked, her voice trembling slightly.

Penny's jaw was set with determination. She looked from the map in her notebook to the distant, brooding cliffs north of the lighthouse. "We have to find that 'back door' ourselves."

"Penny, no! It's too dangerous! And you heard what Jerry said!"

"Jerry isn't here, and a man's life is at stake," Penny retorted. "We won't go into the caves. We'll just go to the cliffs above them. If we see anything, anything at all, we'll run right back for help. We'll need Mr. Skagway to show us the way."

Jake looked from one girl to the other, his expression grim. "It's a bad place. But if old Jim's in trouble... I know a path. Stays high on the bluffs. You can see the entrances to the Widow's caves from there."

Louise looked terrified, but she saw the unshakeable resolve in Penny's eyes. "Oh, alright," she sighed, her loyalty winning out over her fear. "But if we so much as see a spider, I'm turning back."

Under the guise of a "nature walk," the two girls and Jake Skagway set off along the beach, heading north. They left the sandy dunes behind, and the coastline became a rugged wall of rock. Jake led them up a steep, winding path that was barely visible among the gorse and windswept pines.

The higher they climbed, the more spectacular the view became. The entire coastline of Sunset Beach was laid out below them. But Penny had no eyes for the scenery. She was scanning the cliffs below, searching for the cave entrances Jake had described.

"Down there," the old fisherman said, pointing. "See where the water's all churned up? That's the mouth of the main cave. The Whispering Widow."

Penny could see a dark, gaping hole at the waterline, into which the waves surged with a thunderous boom. It was an intimidating sight.

"But he wouldn't be there," Jake continued. "Too obvious. The 'back door' ain't the front door. The real passage is smaller. Harder to spot."

He led them further along the cliff edge. Finally, he stopped. "There."

Below them, half-hidden by a curtain of seaweed and a jumble of fallen rocks, was a much smaller opening. It looked like little more than a dark crack in the cliff face. It was a place one could easily miss from the sea, but it was clear that a small boat could slip inside during high tide.

They crouched behind a cluster of bushes, watching. For a long time, there was nothing but the sound of the wind and the waves. Louise was beginning to fidget.

"Maybe we were wrong, Penny," she whispered. "There's nothing here."

"Quiet!" Penny hissed. "Listen!"

Faintly, carried on the wind, came a sound from the direction of the smaller cave. It was a man's voice, speaking in a sharp, angry tone. The words were German.

The girls exchanged a wide-eyed glance. They were right.

Slowly, cautiously, Penny peered over the edge of the cliff. The angle was difficult, but she could just make out a sliver of the scene below. A small inflatable raft was pulled up on a rocky ledge just inside the cave's mouth. A man, whom Penny instantly recognized as the dark-haired stranger she had seen on the beach with Mrs. Deline, was tying a rope around another man, who was slumped against the cave wall. It was Jim McCoy. He was alive!

The spy, Karl Richter, worked quickly, his movements efficient and ruthless. He was clearly preparing to leave.

"We have to get help!" Louise gasped, tugging on Penny's arm.

"There's no time!" Penny whispered back, her mind racing. "By the time we get back to the hotel and convince Jerry, he'll be gone!"

Her eyes darted around, searching for a solution, anything that could stop him. Her gaze fell upon a pile of loose stones and pebbles at the cliff's edge. An idea, reckless and desperate, flashed into her mind. It was a trick as old as the hills.

"Mr. Skagway," she whispered urgently. "How well does this cliff carry sound?"

"Echoes like a drum," the old man replied, understanding dawning in his eyes.

"Good," Penny said. "Louise, you have the loudest scream I know. When I give the signal, I want you to scream for help as loudly as you can. Mr. Skagway, you shout too. Make it sound like there are a dozen people up here!"

"What are you going to do?" Louise asked, terrified.

"Create a diversion," Penny said, her voice tight with excitement. She grabbed a handful of small stones. "Just like Mrs. Deline did. Now! Get ready!"

She took a deep breath. "Now!"

Louise let out a piercing shriek. At the same moment, Jake Skagway began to bellow, his powerful voice echoing off the rock face. "They're in the cave! Surround them! Don't let them escape!"

As their cries filled the air, Penny began to throw the pebbles, one by one, into the water on the far side of the cave entrance. They made a series of distinct splashes. *Plink. Plonk. Splash.*

Down below, Karl Richter froze. He looked up, his face a mask of alarm. The shouts seemed to be coming from everywhere at once. The splashes sounded like men jumping into the water to cut off his escape. He was trapped!

In that moment of indecision, Jim McCoy, who had been feigning unconsciousness, acted. With a surge of strength, he threw his weight backwards, knocking the unprepared spy off balance. Richter stumbled, and McCoy scrambled away from him, toward the back of the cave.

Enraged, Richter drew a small pistol and turned to pursue the lighthouse keeper. He never got the chance.

A new voice, sharp and authoritative, cut through the air. "Drop it, Richter! Federal agents!"

Penny peered over the edge again. Jerry Livingston and two of his men were on the rocks near the cave mouth, their own guns drawn. They must have followed the Coast Guard search party and heard the commotion.

Checkmated, Karl Richter slowly raised his hands in surrender.

Later, as a shaken but grateful Jim McCoy was being helped back toward the hotel, Jerry Livingston walked over to where Penny, Louise, and Jake were standing.

"I ought to be angry with you, Penny," he said, but he couldn't keep a note of admiration out of his voice. "You directly disobeyed an order."

"But we were right!" Penny said.

"Yes, you were right," Jerry admitted. "McCoy confirmed it. He'd seen Richter signaling a boat from the shore a few nights ago and got suspicious. He put the map together as a set of notes for himself to investigate the 'back door' caves. Richter caught him and was holding him until a submarine rendezvous tonight. Your little sound and light show... well, it probably saved McCoy's life. It certainly kept Richter busy until my men could get into position."

He shook his head, a wry smile playing on his lips. "The Voice from the Cave, and now the Echoes from the Cliff. You have a talent for unconventional warfare, young lady."

"Does this mean the case is finally closed?" Louise asked hopefully.

"With Richter and his accomplices in custody, and Deline's network shattered, yes," Jerry confirmed. "The coast is clear."

That evening, as the sun set in a blaze of orange and pink, Penny stood once more on the veranda, looking out at the lighthouse. Its bright, steady beam swept across the darkening water in a reassuring arc. The light was on. All was right with the world.

"You know, darling," Louise said, coming to stand beside her. "For a 'dead place', this has been a rather lively vacation."

Penny laughed. "It certainly has," she agreed. The capture of the spies, the rescue of the lighthouse keeper... it was almost more excitement than one girl could hope for. She felt a deep sense of satisfaction. But even as she watched the peaceful scene, a familiar, restless spark ignited within her. The world was a big place, full of puzzles to solve and mysteries to uncover. Sunset Beach had been wonderful, but tomorrow they would be heading home. And she couldn't help but wonder what adventure was waiting for her there.

The next morning, the sun rose on a quiet, peaceful Sunset Beach. The sky was scrubbed clean by the previous day's storm and the sea was a placid, welcoming blue. Jerry Livingston drove the girls to the small station a few miles from the coast to catch the morning train back to Riverview.
"You'll write, won't you, Jerry?" Penny asked as they stood on the platform, the train hissing impatiently.
"Of course," he promised, his smile warm. "And if you ever decide to give up the newspaper business, the government could use a girl with your talents for stirring things up."
"I think I'd rather report on the action than create it," Louise said fervently, earning a laugh from the young officer. "This vacation has been quite enough excitement for me."
"Don't listen to her," Penny grinned. "We had a wonderful time. Just be sure to send us a clipping from the city paper when the full story of Richter's spy ring breaks."
"It's a deal," Jerry agreed, shaking their hands. "Have a safe trip, girls. Try to stay out of trouble."
"We'll try!" Penny called back as they climbed aboard the train. She waved from the window until Jerry was just a speck on the platform.
The train lurched into motion, and soon the coastal landscape gave way to rolling fields and tidy little towns. Louise settled back into the plush velvet seat with a contented sigh. "Home," she said happily. "No spies, no caves, no hidden packages. Just peace and quiet."
"It is nice," Penny admitted, but her eyes were already restlessly scanning the other passengers in their car. The thrill of the chase was still fresh in her mind, and the prospect of a long, uneventful train ride seemed terribly dull.
Her gaze fell upon a curious pair seated several rows ahead of them. One was a frail, elderly gentleman with a cloud of white hair and spectacles perched on the end of his nose. He clutched a worn leather portfolio to his chest as if it contained the crown jewels. The other was a sharp featured, irritable looking man in a dark business suit. The two were engaged in a low, tense conversation.
"Now what do you suppose they're talking about?" Penny murmured, leaning forward slightly.
"Probably the weather, or the price of corn," Louise replied, opening a magazine. "Not everything is a national secret, darling."
"The man in the suit looks like a vulture," Penny persisted. "And the old gentleman seems so distressed. Look how he's holding that portfolio. I'll bet a cookie it contains something terribly important, and the other man is trying to get it from him."
"You have an amazing talent for inventing dramas, Penny. For all you know, he's a salesman who won't take no for an answer."
"Maybe," Penny conceded, but she continued to watch them. After a few more minutes of strained conversation, the man in the suit, with an expression of extreme annoyance, stood up and returned to his own seat across the aisle. The elderly gentleman let out a long, shaky breath and pressed the portfolio even closer. A young woman with wide, anxious eyes and neatly pinned brown hair, seated alone a row behind the old man, glanced at him with a look of concern before quickly turning her gaze to the window.
Penny filed the observation away. The cast of characters was certainly interesting, even if the play had not yet begun. She tried to read a book, but her mind kept wandering back to the old man and his precious portfolio.
An hour later, the train whistle shrieked, and the bright afternoon sunshine was abruptly swallowed by the yawning mouth of a long tunnel. The electric lights in the carriage flickered, casting eerie shadows that danced for a moment before dying completely, plunging the car into absolute blackness.
There were a few nervous gasps from the passengers. A baby began to cry.
"I hate tunnels," Louise said, her voice sounding very close in the dark.
"It won't be for long," Penny assured her.
The darkness was thick and disorienting. The rhythmic clatter of the wheels on the track was the only constant sound. Then, through the din, Penny heard a short, sharp cry from the front of the car, followed by a confused shuffling sound. Before she could comment on it, the lights flickered back to life, at first a dim orange, then a steady, reassuring white as the train shot out of the tunnel and back into the daylight.
Passengers blinked, adjusting their eyes. Everything seemed as it was before. But then a panicked voice cried out, "It's gone! It's gone!"
It was the elderly gentleman. He was half standing, his hands patting his empty lap and the seat beside him. His spectacles were askew, and his face was a mask of pure terror. "My portfolio! It's been stolen!"
Immediately, the car was abuzz with excitement. The conductor, a portly man with a perpetually weary expression, came bustling down the aisle. "What's all this? What's the trouble, sir?"
"My portfolio!" the old man repeated, his voice trembling. "It was right here on my lap. The lights went out, and someone took it!"
The conductor sighed. "Now, now, sir. Are you sure you didn't just misplace it? Perhaps it slipped to the floor." He bent down with a groan to peer under the seat, but found nothing.
Penny was already on her feet, her eyes darting around the car. Her first suspect was obvious. The sharp featured man in the business suit, Mr. Vulture, was looking on with an expression that was more annoyed than surprised. He hadn't moved from his seat.
"I'll bet he took it!" Penny whispered fiercely to Louise. "He was arguing with him earlier!"
"Penny, you can't just accuse people!" Louise hissed, pulling at her friend's sleeve. "It was pitch black. It could have been anyone."
"It was him," Penny insisted, her mind racing. The thief had to be someone who knew what was in the portfolio and who was close enough to grab it in the confusion.
The conductor's search proved fruitless. "I'm sorry, sir," he said, straightening up. "There's nothing I can do until we reach the next station. I'll have to file a report. Things do get lost on trains, you know."
"Lost? It wasn't lost, it was stolen!" the old man insisted, sinking back into his seat, looking utterly defeated. The young woman with the anxious eyes watched him, her hands twisting a handkerchief in her lap. She looked as if she wanted to say something, but remained silent.
"This is terrible," Louise murmured. "That poor man."
"We have to do something," Penny declared. "The conductor is useless. If we wait until the next station, the thief will be long gone with that portfolio."
"And what, exactly, do you propose we do?" Louise asked warily. "We can't very well search everyone's luggage."
"Not everyone's," Penny said, her gaze fixed on the businessman. "Just his."
She walked purposefully down the aisle and stopped beside the man's seat. "Pardon me," she said, in her most polite voice. "But you were speaking with that gentleman earlier. Did you happen to see anything when the lights went out?"
The man looked up from his newspaper, his eyes cold and dismissive. "I saw nothing. It was dark," he snapped. "Now if you'll excuse me, I'm trying to read."
"Of course," Penny said, though her conviction only hardened. His rudeness was almost an admission of guilt! As she turned away, she let her eyes sweep the floor around his seat. Tucked partially under the leg of the seat opposite him was a small, metallic object. With a swift, subtle movement, she bent as if to tie her shoe and scooped it up. It was a luggage claim ticket, not for the railway, but for the Riverview Bus Terminal.
She returned to her seat and showed the ticket to Louise. "Look what I found by his seat."
"A claim ticket? What does it prove?"
"It proves he's planning to be somewhere else! Maybe he plans to get off the train and send the portfolio on by bus so he won't be caught with it," Penny theorized excitedly. "Or maybe he's having it picked up by an accomplice!"
"Or maybe he just dropped it," Louise sighed. "Honestly, Penny, you're building a whole case on a rude man and a lost ticket."
"I'm going to talk to the old gentleman," Penny decided, ignoring her friend's skepticism. "Maybe he can tell us who he is, and why that portfolio is so important."
She approached the man's seat gently. The young woman looked up, startled, as Penny knelt by his chair. "Excuse me, sir," Penny began softly. "My name is Penny Parker. I couldn't help but overhear what happened. I'm dreadfully sorry about your portfolio."
The old man looked at her, his eyes bleary with distress. "Thank you, my dear. It's very kind of you. But it's gone. My whole life's work... gone."
"My father is a newspaper publisher," Penny explained. "Sometimes we're able to help with things like this. What was in the portfolio, if you don't mind my asking?"
The man hesitated, then seemed to make a decision. "My name is Professor Thaddeus Pemberton," he said. "The portfolio contained the complete schematics and research notes for an invention I have been perfecting for twenty years. A new type of hydro-dynamic engine."
"An engine!" Penny exclaimed.
"Yes. One that could revolutionize shipping, and perhaps even aviation. It is my legacy." He glanced fearfully toward the businessman. "That man, Mr. Croft, is a representative for a large manufacturing concern. He has been trying to force me to sell my patent for a fraction of its worth. I refused him, and now... now he has taken it."
"That's just what I thought!" Penny declared. "Mr. Croft stole your plans!"
At the mention of the name, the young woman seated behind the professor flinched.
"The conductor won't do anything," Professor Pemberton lamented. "By the time we reach Riverview, Croft will be gone, and my work will be lost to me forever."
"Not if I can help it," Penny said with grim determination. She returned to Louise, her mind buzzing with a dozen daring, and probably foolish, plans.
"He's an inventor, Lou! And that man, Croft, stole his plans for a new kind of engine!"
"So your wild theory was right," Louise admitted, impressed in spite of herself. "But that still doesn't tell us how to get the portfolio back. It's probably hidden in his luggage in the baggage car."
"No," Penny reasoned. "He wouldn't risk that. The conductor might search it. It has to be with him. In his suitcase, or maybe even in that big overcoat of his."
They watched as Mr. Croft folded his newspaper, picked up a small valise from the overhead rack, and headed toward the dining car.
"This is our chance!" Penny whispered. "While he's gone, I can search his seat!"
"Penny, no! You can't! What if he comes back?"
"You'll be my lookout," Penny said, already moving. "Just give me a signal if he starts this way."
Before Louise could protest further, Penny had slipped across the aisle. Her heart hammered against her ribs as she ran her hands over the seat cushions and along the space between the seat and the wall of the train. Nothing. She peered into the pocket on the back of the seat in front. Just a railroad timetable and a discarded candy wrapper. She glanced nervously toward the dining car. There was no sign of Croft.
Her eyes fell on the heavy overcoat he had left folded on his seat. It was a desperate chance. Taking a deep breath, she lifted the coat. It felt heavy, but not bulky. She quickly felt the pockets. One held a pair of leather gloves, the other a train ticket. There was no stiff, rectangular portfolio.
Disappointed, she carefully placed the coat back exactly as it had been. Her search had turned up nothing. She was just sliding back into her own seat when Louise gave a sharp, "Ahem!"
Mr. Croft was returning. He strode down the aisle, his face set in its usual sour expression, and sat down without a second glance. Penny let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding.
"Nothing," she whispered to Louise. "I found absolutely nothing."
"I'm glad," Louise whispered back. "That was entirely too risky. My heart is pounding."
"But where can it be?" Penny fretted. "He has to have it somewhere."
She leaned her head against the window, watching the landscape fly by. They were only an hour or so from Riverview now. Time was running out. She thought about the moment the portfolio had vanished. The total darkness. The cry. The shuffling.
Her eyes drifted to the other players in the little drama. Professor Pemberton sat slumped in his seat, the picture of despair. And then there was the young woman. She was still twisting her handkerchief, her eyes darting from the professor to Mr. Croft, and then, to Penny's surprise, to her. When their eyes met, the young woman looked away quickly, a blush creeping up her neck.
An idea, sudden and strange, sparked in Penny's mind. The woman had been just as tense as the professor. She had been watching everyone. What if...?
"Louise," Penny said slowly. "I've been thinking about this all wrong."
"What do you mean?"
"We've been so focused on Mr. Croft. He's the obvious suspect. But what if the obvious suspect is the wrong one?"
"But the professor said Croft was trying to steal his invention."
"He was trying to buy it for a low price," Penny corrected. "That's not the same as being a thief. He's unpleasant, but maybe he isn't a criminal. What if someone else took the portfolio?"
"Who? The conductor?"
"No. Someone who was also worried about Mr. Croft. Someone who wanted to protect the professor." Penny's gaze was fixed on the anxious young woman. "Someone like a friend. Or a relative."
On an impulse, Penny stood up and walked over to the young woman's seat. "I'm Penny Parker," she said quietly. "You seem very concerned for Professor Pemberton."
The woman looked up, her brown eyes wide with alarm. "He... he is an old friend of the family," she stammered.
"I see," Penny said, her voice gentle but firm. "It was very dark in that tunnel. And things became so confused. It must have been very frightening for the professor."
The woman nodded, unable to speak. She clutched her handkerchief so tightly her knuckles were white.
"A person might do something drastic to protect someone they care about," Penny continued, watching her carefully. "Especially if they thought a man like Mr. Croft was about to get his hands on something valuable. A person might even decide to secure that valuable thing themselves, just until the danger was past."
The young woman's composure finally crumbled. Tears welled in her eyes. "I didn't know what else to do!" she whispered, her voice choked with panic. "I'm his granddaughter, Evelyn Vance. I saw Croft pressuring him. I was so afraid Grandfather would give in, or that Croft would find a way to take the plans. When the lights went out... I just acted. I reached over and took the portfolio. I was going to give it back to him as soon as Croft was gone."
"You took it!" Penny exclaimed in a low voice. Louise, who had crept closer to listen, gasped.
"Then where is it?" Penny demanded. "Give it back to him now! He's sick with worry."
Evelyn Vance shook her head, a fresh wave of panic on her face. "I can't! That's the problem! When the lights came on and he shouted, I panicked. I knew the conductor would come, and I thought I'd be searched. I had to hide it."
"Hide it where?"
"There's a small supply closet for linens near the back of the car," she confessed miserably. "I excused myself a few minutes after the tunnel, pretending to go to the washroom. I slipped it in there, behind a stack of towels."
"And you haven't been back to get it?"
"I was too afraid! Croft keeps watching me. I think he's suspicious of me too. What if he saw me? What do we do?"
"We're going to get it back," Penny said, her mind already working. "Louise, you stay here and keep an eye on Croft. Miss Vance, you need to create a diversion. Go talk to the conductor. Ask him a long, complicated question about the train schedule. Anything to draw his attention and Croft's to the front of the car."
Evelyn nodded, wiping her eyes. "All right. I'll try."
Taking a deep, steadying breath, Evelyn stood and made her way to the front where the conductor was standing. As predicted, her anxious questions immediately drew his full attention. Mr. Croft, ever curious, turned in his seat to watch the exchange.
"Now's our chance, Lou!" Penny urged.
"Me?" Louise squeaked. "Why me?"
"Because you're less suspicious! Just walk to the back of the car as if you're stretching your legs. The closet door should be unlocked. Get the portfolio and bring it back. Quickly!"
Seeing the logic, Louise took a shaky breath and stood up. She ambled down the aisle, trying to look casual. She glanced out the window, smoothed her skirt, and did a very convincing imitation of a bored passenger. Penny held her breath as Louise reached the back of the car and paused by the small, unmarked closet door. The handle turned. The door opened a crack. Louise slipped her hand inside. A moment later, the door clicked shut and Louise was walking back, her expression carefully neutral. Tucked under her arm, partially concealed by her magazine, was a worn leather portfolio.
She slid into her seat just as Evelyn Vance finished her conversation and returned to hers. Mr. Croft had turned back to his newspaper, apparently having lost interest.
"You did it!" Penny breathed.
"My heart nearly jumped out of my chest," Louise whispered back, handing the portfolio to Penny.
Penny didn't hesitate. She walked directly to Professor Pemberton's seat. "Professor," she said, holding out the leather case. "I believe this is yours."
The old man stared at the portfolio as if it were an apparition. He took it with trembling hands, his mouth opening and closing without a sound. He fumbled with the clasp, opened it, and saw his papers lying safe and secure inside. Tears of relief streamed down his wrinkled cheeks.
"But how... where...?" he stammered, looking at Penny with awe.
"Let's just say it was misplaced in the confusion," Penny said with a smile, glancing meaningfully at Evelyn, who gave a small, grateful nod.
At that moment, Mr. Croft stood up. The train was beginning to slow as it approached the outskirts of Riverview. He had seen the portfolio's return. His face was a thundercloud. He took a step toward the professor.
"So, you had it all along," he sneered at Evelyn. "A clever little trick." He turned his cold eyes back to the professor. "This isn't over, Pemberton. My company will have that patent."
"You will have nothing, sir!" Professor Pemberton declared, his voice suddenly strong and clear. Bolstered by the return of his life's work, the frail man seemed to grow in stature. "My granddaughter and I will see my engine manufactured by an honest firm. Now, I will thank you to leave us alone."
Croft looked as if he might argue, but the conductor was now approaching, his eyes narrowed with suspicion at the confrontation. Defeated, Croft snatched his coat and valise and stalked off toward the exit, ready to disembark.
As the train finally pulled into the Riverview station, Professor Pemberton and a very relieved Evelyn Vance couldn't thank the girls enough.
"You are a remarkable young woman, Miss Parker," the professor beamed. "Truly remarkable. You have not just saved my work; you have saved my faith in people."
"It was nothing," Penny said, blushing with pleasure. "I love a good puzzle."
"Well, I for one am ready for a puzzle with fewer angry businessmen and trips to a linen closet," Louise commented as they stepped onto the familiar platform and spotted Penny's father, Anthony Parker, waiting for them.
"There you are, girls!" he called out, enveloping Penny in a hug. "I was beginning to think you'd decided to stay at the beach. How was the rest of your trip?"
Penny grinned at Louise, a familiar twinkle in her eye. "Oh, mostly quiet," she said. "But Dad, have I got a story for you!"

The train lurched into motion, and soon the coastal landscape gave way to rolling fields and tidy little towns. Louise settled back into the plush velvet seat with a contented sigh. "Home," she said happily. "No spies, no caves, no hidden packages. Just peace and quiet."
"It is nice," Penny admitted, but her eyes were already restlessly scanning the other passengers in their car. The thrill of the chase was still fresh in her mind, and the prospect of a long, uneventful train ride seemed terribly dull.
Her gaze fell upon a curious pair seated several rows ahead of them. One was a frail, elderly gentleman with a cloud of white hair and spectacles perched on the end of his nose. He clutched a worn leather portfolio to his chest as if it contained the crown jewels. The other was a sharp featured, irritable looking man in a dark business suit. The two were engaged in a low, tense conversation.
"Now what do you suppose they're talking about?" Penny murmured, leaning forward slightly.
"Probably the weather, or the price of corn," Louise replied, opening a magazine. "Not everything is a national secret, darling."
"The man in the suit looks like a vulture," Penny persisted. "And the old gentleman seems so distressed. Look how he's holding that portfolio. I'll bet a cookie it contains something terribly important, and the other man is trying to get it from him."
"You have an amazing talent for inventing dramas, Penny. For all you know, he's a salesman who won't take no for an answer."
"Maybe," Penny conceded, but she continued to watch them. After a few more minutes of strained conversation, the man in the suit, with an expression of extreme annoyance, stood up and returned to his own seat across the aisle. The elderly gentleman let out a long, shaky breath and pressed the portfolio even closer. A young woman with wide, anxious eyes and neatly pinned brown hair, seated alone a row behind the old man, glanced at him with a look of concern before quickly turning her gaze to the window.
Penny filed the observation away. The cast of characters was certainly interesting, even if the play had not yet begun. She tried to read a book, but her mind kept wandering back to the old man and his precious portfolio.
An hour later, the train whistle shrieked, and the bright afternoon sunshine was abruptly swallowed by the yawning mouth of a long tunnel. The electric lights in the carriage flickered, casting eerie shadows that danced for a moment before dying completely, plunging the car into absolute blackness.
There were a few nervous gasps from the passengers. A baby began to cry.
"I hate tunnels," Louise said, her voice sounding very close in the dark.
"It won't be for long," Penny assured her.
The darkness was thick and disorienting. The rhythmic clatter of the wheels on the track was the only constant sound. Then, through the din, Penny heard a short, sharp cry from the front of the car, followed by a confused shuffling sound. Before she could comment on it, the lights flickered back to life, at first a dim orange, then a steady, reassuring white as the train shot out of the tunnel and back into the daylight.
Passengers blinked, adjusting their eyes. Everything seemed as it was before. But then a panicked voice cried out, "It's gone! It's gone!"
It was the elderly gentleman. He was half standing, his hands patting his empty lap and the seat beside him. His spectacles were askew, and his face was a mask of pure terror. "My portfolio! It's been stolen!"
Immediately, the car was abuzz with excitement. The conductor, a portly man with a perpetually weary expression, came bustling down the aisle. "What's all this? What's the trouble, sir?"
"My portfolio!" the old man repeated, his voice trembling. "It was right here on my lap. The lights went out, and someone took it!"
The conductor sighed. "Now, now, sir. Are you sure you didn't just misplace it? Perhaps it slipped to the floor." He bent down with a groan to peer under the seat, but found nothing.
Penny was already on her feet, her eyes darting around the car. Her first suspect was obvious. The sharp featured man in the business suit, Mr. Vulture, was looking on with an expression that was more annoyed than surprised. He hadn't moved from his seat.
"I'll bet he took it!" Penny whispered fiercely to Louise. "He was arguing with him earlier!"
"Penny, you can't just accuse people!" Louise hissed, pulling at her friend's sleeve. "It was pitch black. It could have been anyone."
"It was him," Penny insisted, her mind racing. The thief had to be someone who knew what was in the portfolio and who was close enough to grab it in the confusion.
The conductor's search proved fruitless. "I'm sorry, sir," he said, straightening up. "There's nothing I can do until we reach the next station. I'll have to file a report. Things do get lost on trains, you know."
"Lost? It wasn't lost, it was stolen!" the old man insisted, sinking back into his seat, looking utterly defeated. The young woman with the anxious eyes watched him, her hands twisting a handkerchief in her lap. She looked as if she wanted to say something, but remained silent.
"This is terrible," Louise murmured. "That poor man."
"We have to do something," Penny declared. "The conductor is useless. If we wait until the next station, the thief will be long gone with that portfolio."
"And what, exactly, do you propose we do?" Louise asked warily. "We can't very well search everyone's luggage."
"Not everyone's," Penny said, her gaze fixed on the businessman. "Just his."
She walked purposefully down the aisle and stopped beside the man's seat. "Pardon me," she said, in her most polite voice. "But you were speaking with that gentleman earlier. Did you happen to see anything when the lights went out?"
The man looked up from his newspaper, his eyes cold and dismissive. "I saw nothing. It was dark," he snapped. "Now if you'll excuse me, I'm trying to read."
"Of course," Penny said, though her conviction only hardened. His rudeness was almost an admission of guilt! As she turned away, she let her eyes sweep the floor around his seat. Tucked partially under the leg of the seat opposite him was a small, metallic object. With a swift, subtle movement, she bent as if to tie her shoe and scooped it up. It was a luggage claim ticket, not for the railway, but for the Riverview Bus Terminal.
She returned to her seat and showed the ticket to Louise. "Look what I found by his seat."
"A claim ticket? What does it prove?"
"It proves he's planning to be somewhere else! Maybe he plans to get off the train and send the portfolio on by bus so he won't be caught with it," Penny theorized excitedly. "Or maybe he's having it picked up by an accomplice!"
"Or maybe he just dropped it," Louise sighed. "Honestly, Penny, you're building a whole case on a rude man and a lost ticket."
"I'm going to talk to the old gentleman," Penny decided, ignoring her friend's skepticism. "Maybe he can tell us who he is, and why that portfolio is so important."
She approached the man's seat gently. The young woman looked up, startled, as Penny knelt by his chair. "Excuse me, sir," Penny began softly. "My name is Penny Parker. I couldn't help but overhear what happened. I'm dreadfully sorry about your portfolio."
The old man looked at her, his eyes bleary with distress. "Thank you, my dear. It's very kind of you. But it's gone. My whole life's work... gone."
"My father is a newspaper publisher," Penny explained. "Sometimes we're able to help with things like this. What was in the portfolio, if you don't mind my asking?"
The man hesitated, then seemed to make a decision. "My name is Professor Thaddeus Pemberton," he said. "The portfolio contained the complete schematics and research notes for an invention I have been perfecting for twenty years. A new type of hydro-dynamic engine."
"An engine!" Penny exclaimed.
"Yes. One that could revolutionize shipping, and perhaps even aviation. It is my legacy." He glanced fearfully toward the businessman. "That man, Mr. Croft, is a representative for a large manufacturing concern. He has been trying to force me to sell my patent for a fraction of its worth. I refused him, and now... now he has taken it."
"That's just what I thought!" Penny declared. "Mr. Croft stole your plans!"
At the mention of the name, the young woman seated behind the professor flinched.
"The conductor won't do anything," Professor Pemberton lamented. "By the time we reach Riverview, Croft will be gone, and my work will be lost to me forever."
"Not if I can help it," Penny said with grim determination. She returned to Louise, her mind buzzing with a dozen daring, and probably foolish, plans.
"He's an inventor, Lou! And that man, Croft, stole his plans for a new kind of engine!"
"So your wild theory was right," Louise admitted, impressed in spite of herself. "But that still doesn't tell us how to get the portfolio back. It's probably hidden in his luggage in the baggage car."
"No," Penny reasoned. "He wouldn't risk that. The conductor might search it. It has to be with him. In his suitcase, or maybe even in that big overcoat of his."
They watched as Mr. Croft folded his newspaper, picked up a small valise from the overhead rack, and headed toward the dining car.
"This is our chance!" Penny whispered. "While he's gone, I can search his seat!"
"Penny, no! You can't! What if he comes back?"
"You'll be my lookout," Penny said, already moving. "Just give me a signal if he starts this way."
Before Louise could protest further, Penny had slipped across the aisle. Her heart hammered against her ribs as she ran her hands over the seat cushions and along the space between the seat and the wall of the train. Nothing. She peered into the pocket on the back of the seat in front. Just a railroad timetable and a discarded candy wrapper. She glanced nervously toward the dining car. There was no sign of Croft.
Her eyes fell on the heavy overcoat he had left folded on his seat. It was a desperate chance. Taking a deep breath, she lifted the coat. It felt heavy, but not bulky. She quickly felt the pockets. One held a pair of leather gloves, the other a train ticket. There was no stiff, rectangular portfolio.
Disappointed, she carefully placed the coat back exactly as it had been. Her search had turned up nothing. She was just sliding back into her own seat when Louise gave a sharp, "Ahem!"
Mr. Croft was returning. He strode down the aisle, his face set in its usual sour expression, and sat down without a second glance. Penny let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding.
"Nothing," she whispered to Louise. "I found absolutely nothing."
"I'm glad," Louise whispered back. "That was entirely too risky. My heart is pounding."
"But where can it be?" Penny fretted. "He has to have it somewhere."
She leaned her head against the window, watching the landscape fly by. They were only an hour or so from Riverview now. Time was running out. She thought about the moment the portfolio had vanished. The total darkness. The cry. The shuffling.
Her eyes drifted to the other players in the little drama. Professor Pemberton sat slumped in his seat, the picture of despair. And then there was the young woman. She was still twisting her handkerchief, her eyes darting from the professor to Mr. Croft, and then, to Penny's surprise, to her. When their eyes met, the young woman looked away quickly, a blush creeping up her neck.
An idea, sudden and strange, sparked in Penny's mind. The woman had been just as tense as the professor. She had been watching everyone. What if...?
"Louise," Penny said slowly. "I've been thinking about this all wrong."
"What do you mean?"
"We've been so focused on Mr. Croft. He's the obvious suspect. But what if the obvious suspect is the wrong one?"
"But the professor said Croft was trying to steal his invention."
"He was trying to buy it for a low price," Penny corrected. "That's not the same as being a thief. He's unpleasant, but maybe he isn't a criminal. What if someone else took the portfolio?"
"Who? The conductor?"
"No. Someone who was also worried about Mr. Croft. Someone who wanted to protect the professor." Penny's gaze was fixed on the anxious young woman. "Someone like a friend. Or a relative."
On an impulse, Penny stood up and walked over to the young woman's seat. "I'm Penny Parker," she said quietly. "You seem very concerned for Professor Pemberton."
The woman looked up, her brown eyes wide with alarm. "He... he is an old friend of the family," she stammered.
"I see," Penny said, her voice gentle but firm. "It was very dark in that tunnel. And things became so confused. It must have been very frightening for the professor."
The woman nodded, unable to speak. She clutched her handkerchief so tightly her knuckles were white.
"A person might do something drastic to protect someone they care about," Penny continued, watching her carefully. "Especially if they thought a man like Mr. Croft was about to get his hands on something valuable. A person might even decide to secure that valuable thing themselves, just until the danger was past."
The young woman's composure finally crumbled. Tears welled in her eyes. "I didn't know what else to do!" she whispered, her voice choked with panic. "I'm his granddaughter, Evelyn Vance. I saw Croft pressuring him. I was so afraid Grandfather would give in, or that Croft would find a way to take the plans. When the lights went out... I just acted. I reached over and took the portfolio. I was going to give it back to him as soon as Croft was gone."
"You took it!" Penny exclaimed in a low voice. Louise, who had crept closer to listen, gasped.
"Then where is it?" Penny demanded. "Give it back to him now! He's sick with worry."
Evelyn Vance shook her head, a fresh wave of panic on her face. "I can't! That's the problem! When the lights came on and he shouted, I panicked. I knew the conductor would come, and I thought I'd be searched. I had to hide it."
"Hide it where?"
"There's a small supply closet for linens near the back of the car," she confessed miserably. "I excused myself a few minutes after the tunnel, pretending to go to the washroom. I slipped it in there, behind a stack of towels."
"And you haven't been back to get it?"
"I was too afraid! Croft keeps watching me. I think he's suspicious of me too. What if he saw me? What do we do?"
"We're going to get it back," Penny said, her mind already working. "Louise, you stay here and keep an eye on Croft. Miss Vance, you need to create a diversion. Go talk to the conductor. Ask him a long, complicated question about the train schedule. Anything to draw his attention and Croft's to the front of the car."
Evelyn nodded, wiping her eyes. "All right. I'll try."
Taking a deep, steadying breath, Evelyn stood and made her way to the front where the conductor was standing. As predicted, her anxious questions immediately drew his full attention. Mr. Croft, ever curious, turned in his seat to watch the exchange.
"Now's our chance, Lou!" Penny urged.
"Me?" Louise squeaked. "Why me?"
"Because you're less suspicious! Just walk to the back of the car as if you're stretching your legs. The closet door should be unlocked. Get the portfolio and bring it back. Quickly!"
Seeing the logic, Louise took a shaky breath and stood up. She ambled down the aisle, trying to look casual. She glanced out the window, smoothed her skirt, and did a very convincing imitation of a bored passenger. Penny held her breath as Louise reached the back of the car and paused by the small, unmarked closet door. The handle turned. The door opened a crack. Louise slipped her hand inside. A moment later, the door clicked shut and Louise was walking back, her expression carefully neutral. Tucked under her arm, partially concealed by her magazine, was a worn leather portfolio.
She slid into her seat just as Evelyn Vance finished her conversation and returned to hers. Mr. Croft had turned back to his newspaper, apparently having lost interest.
"You did it!" Penny breathed.
"My heart nearly jumped out of my chest," Louise whispered back, handing the portfolio to Penny.
Penny didn't hesitate. She walked directly to Professor Pemberton's seat. "Professor," she said, holding out the leather case. "I believe this is yours."
The old man stared at the portfolio as if it were an apparition. He took it with trembling hands, his mouth opening and closing without a sound. He fumbled with the clasp, opened it, and saw his papers lying safe and secure inside. Tears of relief streamed down his wrinkled cheeks.
"But how... where...?" he stammered, looking at Penny with awe.
"Let's just say it was misplaced in the confusion," Penny said with a smile, glancing meaningfully at Evelyn, who gave a small, grateful nod.
At that moment, Mr. Croft stood up. The train was beginning to slow as it approached the outskirts of Riverview. He had seen the portfolio's return. His face was a thundercloud. He took a step toward the professor.
"So, you had it all along," he sneered at Evelyn. "A clever little trick." He turned his cold eyes back to the professor. "This isn't over, Pemberton. My company will have that patent."
"You will have nothing, sir!" Professor Pemberton declared, his voice suddenly strong and clear. Bolstered by the return of his life's work, the frail man seemed to grow in stature. "My granddaughter and I will see my engine manufactured by an honest firm. Now, I will thank you to leave us alone."
Croft looked as if he might argue, but the conductor was now approaching, his eyes narrowed with suspicion at the confrontation. Defeated, Croft snatched his coat and valise and stalked off toward the exit, ready to disembark.
As the train finally pulled into the Riverview station, Professor Pemberton and a very relieved Evelyn Vance couldn't thank the girls enough.
"You are a remarkable young woman, Miss Parker," the professor beamed. "Truly remarkable. You have not just saved my work; you have saved my faith in people."
"It was nothing," Penny said, blushing with pleasure. "I love a good puzzle."
"Well, I for one am ready for a puzzle with fewer angry businessmen and trips to a linen closet," Louise commented as they stepped onto the familiar platform and spotted Penny's father, Anthony Parker, waiting for them.
"There you are, girls!" he called out, enveloping Penny in a hug. "I was beginning to think you'd decided to stay at the beach. How was the rest of your trip?"
Penny grinned at Louise, a familiar twinkle in her eye. "Oh, mostly quiet," she said. "But Dad, have I got a story for you!"
